text: 189. Bng. udbāsiṇɔ ‘to feel very hot (in summer or in front of a fire)’, Deog. udbās ‘(suf- fering from) great heat’, Baur. udbās ‘blistering heat’. Looks only coincidentally like OIA udbhāsati ‘shines out’. There is a no longer productive prefix ɔd-, ud- in quite a number of other Bng. words which roughly means ‘much’ but whose origin is unclear (e.g. in ɔdṛiāṇɔ ‘to take out more’ ← ṛiāṇɔ ‘to take or bring out, draw’ [only rarely used independently].). The verb stem bās- may derive < OIA bhāsá- ‘light’ (9480)  but the meaning ‘heat’ instead of ‘light’ is geographically limited: Kal. bhas ‘heat’ (in Trail/Cooper but Morgenstierne gives ‘flame’), Ind. bhʌysà̄ ‘briefly heated and subse- quently stored meat’ and loanword Brah. bāsing ‘to be hot, become hot’. Ex. from Bng.: rāt bɔri udbāsiṇɔ aũ etra night whole feel_hot.PP.M.SG I today ‘today I felt very hot the whole night’ na boś āgi kai, udbās lāgɛ not sit.IMP fire near, great_heat attach.PR.3.SG ‘don’t sit near the fire, it is very hot’

text: 217. Bng. ulkɔ, olkɔ ‘a shooting star; firelight’ and ulkɛṇɔ ‘to flame or blaze up’ (cf. p. 218); Garh. ulkā ‘meteor’; Bhal. sānhëlu ‘evening star’ (Kaul [2006 i: 336]) which is a compound < OIA saṁdhá̄- ‘twilight’ (12908) plus OIA uḍu- ‘star’ (1694) (Pa., Pk.) (?); here also Jaun. uḍāv kuria ‘pole star’ (with -āv probably a vālā suffix, second word < a side-form of OIA *kuḍa-¹ ‘boy, son’ [3245]) — Paš. ulík ‘spark’ (Buddruss [1959b: 28]). According to CDIAL, there is one possible modern reflex in Si., which is amazing as the OIA word is documented only lately; note however, S. ulo ‘spark’, G. “uḥlᵃkũ̄ ‘a rain of fire’ (LSI [i, ii: 347]) and M. uḍu ‘a star’ but ulkā ‘a meteor’ (also Ko. and cf. Ko. ulop, ulpā ‘inflammation; passion; heat’ and ulpāi to scorch’ which may derive < OIA LIP ‘inflame, kindle, burn’) which, like the Bng. and perhaps Bhal. forms, is related with OIA ulká̄- ‘meteor’ (2362). Here to be noted are also Deshi Prakrit ukkalo ‘heat’ (Bhayani [1988: 62]) and Ora. ullkā ‘a burn’. Note that there are other remarkable West Pahāṛī and outer language words related to the night sky: Bhal. gu-rot ‘milky way’ (see p. 705), Jaun. viã̄ṇia ‘morning star’ (see p. 714), Jaun. kirkiṭi ‘the Pleiades’ (Z.) (OIA kŕ̥ttikā- [3427], tatsama?), Sirm. “dhanishta” ‘asterism’ (Negi [1969: 433]) cf. OIA dhiṣṇya- with meaning ‘star, asterism (looking like the fire on the side altars)’ given by the astronomer Varāhamihira; Mult. māhõ māhĩã ‘the Gemini’ (O’Brian) a redupli- cation < OIA mithuna- i.a. ‘the sign of the zodiac Gemini’; Ind. pālʌ́ṅg and Jaṭ. palaggh pīhṛā (with second word < OIA pīṭha- ‘stool, bench’ [8222]) both ‘Ursa Major’ (lit.: ‘bedstead [seat]’) < palyaṅka- ‘chair of state, litter; Thronsessel, Tragsessel, Sänfte’ (7964) also found in Mult. and Kgr. as palag pihṛā and khaṭṭ, Garh. khāṭ, Brah. kaṭṭāk ‘Great Bear’ (< OIA kháṭvā- ‘bedstead’ [3781]) ‘con- stellation of Great Bear’, Shahpur dialect of Jaṭ. mã̄jā ‘constellation of Great Bear’ (< OIA mañca- ‘bed’ [9715]) and Kal. šen tári ‘big dipper constellation’ (literally ‘bed star’ with first word < OIA śáyana- ‘bed’). The quoted words have taken this meaning ultimately from Akkadian ereqqu ‘wagon; Ursa major’ (cf. in Europe Charles wain, Wotanswagen, gran carro etc., see p. 584 on more names of stars and asterisms). Some of the words are more or less old tatsamas.

text: 230. Bng. ūr n.f. ‘anger, fury’, uru ‘a flood; a wild bull’ as in uru-suru lagɛ paṇi rɛ (flood- ECHO occur.PP.M.Pl water of) ‘a flood of water came’, ŭ̄rṇɔ ‘to swell, become inflated (e.g., a river, breast); to storm ahead (as warriors or a herd)’ and ura-uriɛ ‘quickly, spontaneously’, Ku. urīṇ ‘to gather (as clouds)’ < OIA údīrte ‘rises’ (1939) (Pa., Pk.) (see there also OIA údīrayati ‘causes to move’) with one modern reflex in Paš to which Garh. ūreṇu ‘to start, initiate’ and ūr ‘start’ ought to be added; here also borrowing into Brah. (h)ūringing ‘to swell up’; the Bng. form uru-suru, which is not a normal echo word, might be influenced by sursuri ‘burbling (of water)’ < OIA sárati ‘flows’ (13250)?

text: 298. OIA kapolá- ‘cheek’ (2755) (Pa., Pk.), whose origin is unclear (see EWA), does not have, according to Turner, modern reflexes (but *kappola- has in Si. and Tor., and see also perhaps ‘prefix-less’ forms p. 659), but they are found in the northwest: Ind. kʌylⁱ1-dá̄n ‘a molar’, Brah. kalik ‘cheek’, Bur./Sh. kaldón ‘molar’. According to Berger dissimilated < *kandón “ear-tooth’, Ohrenzahn’, however, Morgenstierne (1956: 92) correctly considers connection between Paš. kāl-dˈōn ‘back-tooth’ and kalˈāva ‘cheek’, which appears as káḷi ‘cheek’ in Kal. (but note also kálak aṭhi and kályak both ‘jawbone’), khól in Gau., qāl ‘cheek’ in Bro. (Ramaswami [1975: 57]), and probably also in Jaḍ. kalcūnā ‘the temples’ (with unclear second component). Also in Gaw. khiläṇṭˈa, in Paš. keleṇṭho respectively kalavāṇṭek ‘cheek’ (Lehr [2014: 99]), Note that the lemma has also been borrowed into Munda Ju. koɭo danto ‘molar’.

text: 458. Khaś., Marm., Śeu. gelhori, gəlhoṛi, Low Rudh. gəlhoṛa all ‘cheek’ — Ind. mũʌ̀ỹ hargʌỳlⁱ ‘cheek’ (with mũʌ̀ỹ genitive of mũ̄́ ‘cheek’ < OIA múkha- ‘mouth, face’ [10158]), Tor. bogùl ‘cheek’. The forms contain a component which is < OIA galla- ‘cheek’ (4089). Since there is Sh. häróm ‘cheek’, this shows that Khaś. etc. gelhori and Ind. . . . hargʌỳlⁱ are synonym compounds with the other component of unknown origin. Note: There are the similar forms Kal. káḷi ‘cheek’, Paš.DN. kalavāṇṭek ‘cheek’ (Lehr 2014: 99), Brah. kalik ‘cheek’ and Bal. kalak ‘cheek of animals’ which are, however, rather related with Pers. kala ‘the face or cheek’.

text: 468. There is Pog. golam “barley” mentioned by Kaul (2006 i: 243) together with yuvān “wheat”. He points out that this data is from Siddheshwar Varma and that there is apparently “. . . metathesis in the meanings of terms. . . ” because golam goes back to OIA godhú̄ma- ‘wheat’ (4287) and yuvān to OIA yavāní- ‘a kind of bad barley’ (10439). The question is whether the -l- in golam is a reflex of the OIA -dh-, a sound change hitherto only known from Dard and Nuristan languages west of Kashmiri as in Pr. ülüm ‘wheat’. It is also worth pointing to Brah. xōlum ‘wheat’ which Turner (loc. cit.) regards as a borrowing from IA *gōlūm. On more interpretations see Rossi (1979: 155) and Southworth (2005a: 80). Note also M.kas. gōdi ‘wheat’ (an unusual semi-tatsama?) and borrowing into Munda Korwa and Sant. gohom ‘wheat’.

text: 505. The following three closely related lemmata are morphologically differentiated by ċha(r)-/ċhi(r)- and cha(r)-/chi(r)-/chu(r)- versus ċa(r)-/ċi(r)-ċu(r)-- and ca(r)-/cu(r)- versus śa(r)- and ṣi(r)-, thus reflecting three originally closely related allomorphs of one common macro lemma with clear Austro-Asiatic ‘cognates’ as suggested by PMK *[c]rɔk ‘to drip’:  (a) Bng. and Deog. ċhɔṛ-ċhɔṛ ‘dripping, sound of raindrops’ and verbal Bng. ċhiṛpiṛɑṇɔ and Deog. ċhiṛbiṛaɔṇɔ ‘to drizzle continuously’ and perhaps Bng. chiṛmiṛɔ ‘shallow (as water)’, Central Pahāṛī chir- ‘to drip (grain etc.)’, Ku. chaṇchaṇ ‘sound of rain’, N. churra ‘the sound of splashing water’, and chalchali and chulukka in ch. . . mutnu ‘to micturate through fear’ (with verb mutnu < OIA mūtráyati ‘urinates’ [10238]) — Ind. ċhʌ́r-ċhʌr ‘sound of raindrops dripping from the gutter’, Bur. ċhar mań- ‘to drip, squirt’, ċháċhar mań- ‘to trickle’ and ċhúċhur mań- ‘to trickle lightly (rain)’, Sh. ċhar ‘ditto’, Gau. ċhvir ‘drop’, Kal. ċhirċharék ‘to rain lightly, sprinkle, drizzle’, Pr. oċur-, vuċur- ‘spritzen’ — Bun. ċirċir ‘drizzle’ — Sant. cɔrɔ ‘urinate’ and cɔrɔ cɔrɔ ‘sound of falling, passing water’ and char char ‘with a splashing sound’. Perhaps cognate with OIA *kṣarā- ‘melting away; cloud; water’ (3662) (cf. loc. cit. K. char ‘a sprinkle of water etc. from the fingers’). However, the words may also be related with OIA *jhaṭati ‘falls’ (5328) e.g. L. jhaṛaṇ ‘to drip, ooze’; and note Deś. (116,5) ciricirā tathā ciriṃcira jaladhāra. Here probably also Munda jibir jibir, jhibir jhibir ‘to drizzle’ which resembles Deog. ċhiṛbiṛaɔṇɔ. (b) Bng. ċur-ċur or ċuṛ-ċuṛ and Deog. ċuṛkɔ̄ṇɔ or ċūṛṇɔ all ‘sound of leaking water’, and Bng. ċuṛku n.m. ‘drop of water’, Rudh. ˈcruci ‘continuous but gentle trickling or oozing of water’ and cuˈruru ‘a perennial spring’, Ku. curɛ̄n and Garh. curāṇ ‘bad smell of urine’ (with second syllable < OIA ghrāṇá- ‘smelling’ [4531]) — Rp. cyũku ‘urine’, Bun. ċirċir ‘drizzle’ — N. culculi ‘pissing’ — A. sirika (cirikā) ‘drizzle’ — Wkh. čur x̆ak ‘to urinate as baby’ — Ind. čúrčur karʌ́ṽ ‘to urinate’, Bur. ćar ‘to pour’ and ćurućurúu ét- ‘to pee’, Kal. čurụék ‘to drain off, wring out’ and čurụík ‘to leak in a steady stream’, Kho. ċraxˈey- ‘drizzle’, Kamd. ċuňˈi oa ‘urine’ (with ˈoa ‘water’) and c̣ˈař čāpa ‘make the sound of urinating’ (note ċ- versus c̣-); also Bal. čurro and Brah. čurrō ‘urine’ and cf. Psht. čur ‘a furrow or ravine made by running water; a channel; a gutter’. Cf. also Sant. sarsar which also expresses ‘watery’ sounds and which is certainly cognate with Katuic Ngeq carcɛr ‘to drip (as water chute end of the rain trough)’, Bahnaric Mnong creːt creːt ‘drip out little by little’, Khmu cèr ‘to drip’, Monic Nyah Kur crɤ́h-crɤ́h ‘(dripping) continuously (of a liquid)’. (c) Bng. and Deog. śɔr-śɔr ‘pitter-patter (rain)’, Deog. also śor-śor ‘sound of a moun- tain river’, Ku. śãṇśãṇ ‘sound of rain’, Paṭṭ. śəru ‘incessant rain’, Bng. śɔrkaṇɔ ‘to hose urine, milk a cow with force’ (with intensive -k- suffix) — Ind. šʌ́r-šʌr ‘pitter-patter (rain), sound of drizzle, trickle’, K. śār3 ‘a fall of water’ and śŏr ‘the noise of the fall of a stream of water, a splash’, Paš. šor- ‘to flow’, probably Kal. ṣiṣárik ‘to sprinkle’ — P. śarlāṭā ‘gust of rain or wind’ (T. Graham Bailey [1938: 250]; note palatal sibilant) — Par. šurˈšur ‘to murmur, purl’, Mj. šarfā, šarfɔ, Ishk. and Wkh. šoršor, Sang. šāršor, Shgh. šahršahr; Bur. śarśar ‘sound of grain trickling down’ (Berger connects this word with the group under Ind. šʌ́r1 ‘sow; scatter’, but Pers. šarīdan ‘to drop; to flow [as rivers] with a great noise; to pour, trickle, urine’, šaršar ‘flowing or falling water’ and šurrīdan ‘to flow, murmur [as water or any liquid poured out]’ seems closer), Psht. šar, šir ‘pattering of rain’ < Ir. *gžar ? (*gzar ?) ‘to flow (fast?)’? Notes: (a) M. sarvā ‘heavy shower’, M.wār. sər ‘shower (of rain)’ and G. saravā ‘ditto’ are cognate with OIA āsāra-¹ ‘hard shower’ (1491), as is clarified by Deś. (276,9) sarivāo tathā sīharao āsāraḥ, and thus with SAR ‘move’. However, the etymo- logical background of this OIA root is somehow intricate. Therefore I suggest that the M. and G. forms are actually more closely related with Pahāṛī forms mentioned p. 235 sub serɔ, seri ‘an irrigable or irrigated field’. (b) Sub Par. šaršaˈrā ‘waterfall’ Morgenstierne points out that this is a pan- Afghanistan and Persia word. It is synonym with Par. ɣarɣaˈrā ‘cascade; the sound of falling water’ which is also Persian. For etymologically related(?) IA forms see p. 457. (c) Note also (as borrowings?) Korku sirsi ‘to sprinkle with water’, Bondo sisira- ‘to sprinkle’, Bodo-Gadaba sisra ‘to sprinkle with water’.

text: 571. Bng. dzupɔ2 ‘dim (as light)’ (is homonymous with dzupɔ1 n.m. ‘supporting post in stable’ which does not fit semantically with OIA yujyáte ‘is yoked’ [10503, cf. there e.g. Pk. juppaï ‘is joined’] and therefore rather seems to reflect OIA yūpya- ‘fit or suitable for a sacrificial post’), dzupzupɔ ‘very dim, not clear’, dzupāṇɔ ‘to confuse s.o.’, dzupāṭh2 n.m. ‘confusion’ (is homonymous with dzupāṭh1 n.m. ‘a post in the stable’ with same derivation as dzupɔ1 with -āṭh suffix) all < OIA yupyati ‘confuses, obstructs; is concealed’. Note: Bng. dzòpṇɔ ‘to blow a fire’, dzùpzupāṇɔ ‘to flicker (as light, fire)’, Deog. dzhupzhupano ‘to flicker’ do not belong here but derive < OIA *jhapp- ‘sudden movement’ (5336). To the large number of modern reflexes are also to be added Kal. zup ‘suddenly, briefly’, Paš. ǰup ‘jumping’, Brah. ǰupping ‘to jump’.

text: 826. Jaṭ. and P. nich, Si. nicchᵃ, Sh.koh. nĭch all ‘sneeze’ < OIA *nikṣuvati ‘sneezes’ which parallels OIA *vikṣuvati ‘sneezes’ (11654) with modern reflexes in Nuristani, but probably to be added is Paš.DN. baxč- ‘sneeze’. The IA forms starting with n- have a parallel in Psht. nẓai ‘sneeze’ which has also the same root with a different prefix in prac̣ ‘sneeze’ (Wkh. pörš- ‘to sneeze’). Notes: (a) Somewhat similar sounding Dravidian Brah. hiččān ‘sneeze’ and Iranian Par. ˈatsa ‘sneeze’, however, a borrowing < OIA *hañji- ‘sneeze’ (13941a) with a modern parallel in A. hã̄ci (phonet. -s-) ‘sneezing’; related seems also Munda Korku accu ‘to sneeze’ and acchu * sneeze’; Mayrhofer regards the word as an onomatopoeic creation (EWA sub KṢAV ), but considering the great geographic distance between A. and Brah. this is hard to believe. (b) Here probably also B.roh. áĩśśar ‘sneezing’ and áĩśśōn ‘of sneezing’. (c) Iranian Par. pan ‘sneeze’ as in pan-eman dhētan ‘I am sneezing’ (IIFL xi: 280) is perhaps only accidentally similar with onomatopoeic PIE *pneu- ‘sneeze’.
